title: Tank Vehicles
summary: When you need a tank endorsement, how to inspect a tanker, and how surge and a high center of gravity change the way you drive.

sections.heading: When you need a tank endorsement

blocks.text: A tank vehicle carries any liquid or liquid gas in tanks that meet BOTH size tests. The liquid does not have to be hazardous: water and milk count.

rows: Individual rated capacity of more than 119 gallons
Aggregate rated capacity of 1,000 gallons or more
Permanently or temporarily attached to the vehicle or chassis
Endorsement needed for any liquid or gas in qualifying tanks
Endorsement needed only when hauling hazardous materials in liquid or gas form in qualifying tanks

items: One 900-gallon tank: not a tank vehicle (total is under 1,000 gallons).
Two 600-gallon tanks: tank vehicle (each over 119, total 1,200).
Ten 110-gallon tanks: not a tank vehicle (no single tank is over 119 gallons).
Under federal rules, an empty storage tank that is not designed to carry cargo, temporarily attached to a flatbed, does not make the truck a tank vehicle.

rows: Combined tank and hazmat endorsement, for tank drivers hauling hazmat in amounts that require placards

blocks.text: A commercial learner's permit (CLP) holder with an N endorsement carries an X restriction: they may drive only an empty tank vehicle, and never one that held hazmat unless it has been purged of all residue.
Inspect before loading, unloading or driving. Tankers come in many types and sizes, so use the vehicle's operator manual to learn how to inspect yours.

items: Leaks are the most important thing to check on every tanker. Look under and around the vehicle.
Check the tank's body or shell for dents or leaks.
Make sure intake, discharge and cut-off valves are in the correct position before loading, unloading or moving.
Check pipes, connections and hoses for leaks, especially around joints.
Manhole covers must have gaskets and close correctly. Keep vents clear.
If your tank has them, make sure vapor recovery kits, grounding and bonding cables, emergency shut-off systems and built-in fire extinguishers work.
Find out what emergency equipment you must carry, and make sure you have it and it works.

blocks.text: Hauling liquid or gas in a leaking tank is a crime. You will be cited and stopped from driving further, and you may have to pay for the cleanup. Never drive with open valves or manhole covers.

sections.heading: High center of gravity and surge

blocks.text: Bulk liquids are heavy, shift easily and ride high. These two problems, a high center of gravity and liquid movement, are why tank driving takes special skill.

rows: Much of the weight sits high off the road, so the truck is top-heavy and rolls over easily. Tankers can turn over at the posted speed for a curve.
Liquid moving in a partly filled tank. When you stop, the wave hits the end of the tank and pushes the truck in the direction the wave is moving.

blocks.text: On ice or another slippery surface, surge can shove a stopped tanker out into an intersection.
Take highway curves and on- and off-ramps well below the posted speed.

sections.heading: Bulkheads, baffles and smooth bore tanks

rows: Solid walls that divide one tank into several smaller tanks. When loading or unloading compartments, watch weight distribution so you don't put too much weight on the front or rear.
Bulkheads with holes that let liquid flow through. They slow forward-and-back surge, but side-to-side surge still happens and can cause a rollover.

Nothing inside to slow the liquid, so forward-and-back surge is very strong. Usually used for food such as milk, because sanitation rules forbid hard-to-clean baffles. Be extremely careful, especially when starting and stopping.

blocks.text: If you empty the rear compartments first and leave the front ones full, too much weight may end up on the front of the vehicle.

sections.heading: Outage and how much to load

blocks.text: Never load a cargo tank completely full. Liquids expand as they warm, and the room you leave for that expansion is called outage. Different liquids expand by different amounts, so know the outage needed for what you haul.

items: How much the liquid will expand in transit.
The weight of the liquid.
Legal weight limits. A full tank of a dense liquid, such as some acids, may be over the limit, so heavy liquids are often loaded only partly full.
Start, slow down and stop very smoothly. Make smooth turns and lane changes.
Keep steady pressure on the brakes when stopping, and do not release too soon.
Brake far ahead of a stop and increase your following distance.
For a quick stop, use controlled braking (as hard as you can without locking the wheels, with very small steering moves) or stab braking. Do not jam on the brakes.
With stab braking, wait for the wheels to start rolling again (up to one second) before reapplying, or the vehicle will not straighten out.
Slow down before a curve, then accelerate slightly through it.
Wet roads double your normal stopping distance, and an empty tanker may take longer to stop than a full one.

blocks.text: Steering quickly while braking can roll a tanker over. Over-steering, over-accelerating or over-braking can cause a skid; on a tank trailer, skidding drive or trailer wheels can jackknife the rig. When any vehicle skids, act to restore traction to the wheels.

keyPoints: Tank endorsement (N): each tank over 119 gallons AND 1,000 gallons or more in total, any liquid or gas. Class C needs it only for hazmat.
X endorsement = tank plus hazmat for placarded loads; a CLP's X restriction means empty, purged tanks only.
Leaks are the most important inspection item; never drive with open valves or manhole covers.
High center of gravity makes tankers roll easily; take curves and ramps well below the posted speed.
Surge pushes the truck in the direction the wave moves; baffles stop front-to-back surge but not side-to-side.
Smooth bore tanks (often milk) have the strongest surge; be extra careful starting and stopping.
Leave outage for expansion, and watch weight limits with dense liquids.
Drive smoothly, brake early with steady pressure, and use controlled or stab braking in emergencies.
